case_study_insert.main_stem: Northgate Formalwear (NGF) is a private limited company in the formal menswear retail sector, based in Columbus, Ohio, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by David Okafor, it sells suits and office wear through three stores and a growing online shop, operating a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. NGF plans to invest $720,000 in a new automated e-commerce fulfilment centre with computer stock control, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $310,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $24.50, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. NGF faces an online returns problem, with 13.5% of units returned and rising quality complaints.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 800 online shoppers found that 58% would buy formalwear online at least once a year and 46% say free returns are the main reason they choose an online retailer. Fulfilment currently averages 3.5 days per order, and the returns rate stands at 13.5%, compared with 8.2% for in-store purchases. Of 1,200 orders shipped last quarter, 163 were returned. The survey also found that 61% of respondents say online sizing guides would increase their confidence to purchase, and 39% of returns cited 'item too large' or 'item too small' as the reason.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.75%, the fifth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.42 to $14.25 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills across retail. (3) Parcel carrier fuel surcharges have risen 8.0% year-on-year and clothing input costs are up 5.4%, although consumer online apparel spending grew 6.8%.

questions.question_text: NGF plans to fund the new e-commerce fulfilment centre with a ten-year bank loan and retained profit. Explain two advantages for NGF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs NGF no interest and creates no new repayment commitments, so the $270,000 is invested without stretching cash flow at a time when fixed costs already stand at $310,000 a year and the business must service a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid in interest protects NGF's ability to absorb the 5.4% rise in clothing input costs and the 8.0% parcel carrier fuel surcharge while holding the $24.50 selling price against rival online retailers.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral or guarantee, so the automated fulfilment centre is not at risk of repossession if online demand disappoints — a real possibility when 13.5% of units are already returned. Unlike increasing the bank loan, using its own profits also preserves David Okafor's ownership and control, since no lender can attach conditions on how the centre is run, what staff are hired or how quickly the loan must be repaid. Finally, avoiding extra debt strengthens NGF's relationship with its bank, keeping the $450,000 facility available for working capital while the expansion ramps up and the 6.8% growth in online apparel spending is pursued.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NGF's expansion, costs, returns problem and financing decision.

questions.question_text: NGF is launching the online range that will be fulfilled from the new centre. Consider paid search advertising, social media influencer marketing or email marketing to NGF's existing customers. Which should NGF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Paid search advertising: Paid search places NGF at the top of results when shoppers search for terms such as 'buy suit online', capturing high-intent buyers exactly when they are ready to purchase. Spend is measurable through click-through and conversion data and NGF can cap the daily budget. However, bids for retail keywords are highly competitive, and every click costs money even without a sale, straining NGF's resources after committing $720,000 to the centre.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion and lifestyle influencers could showcase NGF's suits to younger professionals, generating aspirational content and quick traffic surges. Its weaknesses are that results compound slowly, influencer credibility varies, and NGF's formalwear buyers skew older than typical influencer audiences, so much of the spend may not convert to the 55,000-unit target.

Email marketing: Emailing existing customers costs very little per message and reaches people who already trust NGF's stores. NGF can promote the launch, free returns and the online sizing guides that 61% of surveyed shoppers say would raise their confidence to buy, and track orders against the 1,200-orders-per-quarter benchmark. Its limitation is reach: it cannot win first-time customers, so awareness growth is capped.

Recommendation: NGF should choose email marketing as the lead channel, supported later by modest paid search. Email is the cheapest, most measurable and best-targeted route to announce the launch to a warm audience and to highlight the free returns valued by 46% of shoppers. Paid search alone is rejected as too expensive against national rivals for a business funding $720,000 of investment, influencer marketing is rejected as poorly matched to formalwear's buyer profile, and neither suits a launch better than a direct message to loyal customers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to NGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NGF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of NGF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why paid search and influencer marketing are rejected.

questions.question_text: NGF's returns rate has reached 13.5% and quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for NGF of using democratic leadership to tackle this problem with its fulfilment team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives NGF's fulfilment employees a voice in how picking, packing and quality checks are organised, satisfying their esteem needs and raising commitment. Workers who help design the size-check and packing routines are more likely to follow them consistently, cutting the error rate that is driving the 13.5% returns rate and the 163 units sent back last quarter.

Point 2: Front-line staff see packing and sizing faults before managers do, so democratic leadership surfaces practical fixes quickly — for example, clearer size labels or more accurate picking against the computer stock control system. Falling returns protect the contribution on each of the 55,000 units NGF sells a year, support the 61% of surveyed shoppers who want better online sizing confidence, and build morale and loyalty in a warehouse team already stretched by festive volumes. Higher involvement also lifts commitment and accuracy across the picking team at exactly the point where the new e-commerce fulfilment centre most needs consistent, motivated pickers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NGF's returns rate, quality complaints and fulfilment operation.

questions.question_text: NGF needs a returns-quality supervisor for the fulfilment centre. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment. Which should NGF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Promoting an experienced picker or packer to returns-quality supervisor is fast and inexpensive, and NGF already knows the candidate's attendance, pace and attitude. The appointee understands the computer stock control system and the layout of the new centre, needs little induction, and the promotion signals to the 60 employees that effort is rewarded, aiding retention in a warehouse role. The drawbacks are that NGF may choose from a small pool, the promoted worker still needs supervisory training, and an internal hire may lack the fresh ideas or formal quality qualifications an external candidate could bring.

External recruitment: Advertising externally widens the pool to trained quality supervisors with formal credentials and experience of other retailers' returns operations, which could inject new standards and audit rigour into a business fighting a 13.5% returns rate with 163 units returned last quarter. However, external recruitment is slower and costlier — advertising, interviewing and induction while the centre is being commissioned — and a newcomer may misread NGF's flat, team-based ways of working or the specifics of its computer stock control system, risking an early mis-hire.

Decision: NGF should choose internal recruitment. The priority is speed and cultural fit during the $720,000 expansion: an internal appointee can be in post before the centre opens, understands the workforce and costs almost nothing in fees. External recruitment is rejected because the $450,000 bank loan is already committed to the investment itself, NGF's most urgent need is someone who knows its e-commerce returns flow from day one, and any gaps in quality-audit skills can be closed later with a short off-the-job course.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to NGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment methods in the context of NGF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of NGF with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, fit and the returns problem.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NGF's management can use its cost and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $310,000 ÷ ($24.50 − $14.50) = $310,000 ÷ $10.00 = 31,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 31,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $24.50 − $14.50 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NGF's management can use this break-even and contribution data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. NGF's managers can compare the 31,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 55,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 24,000 units before committing further capacity in the new e-commerce fulfilment centre.
2. Contribution per unit of $10.00 lets managers model a 10% promotional discount (new price $22.05, contribution $7.55) to test whether the extra volume would still cover the $310,000 fixed costs.
3. Break-even analysis supports the financing plan: managers can check the expanded business covers its $450,000 loan repayments only if output stays comfortably above 31,000 units, informing whether to fix the loan rate now the base rate has risen to 5.75%.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($310,000 ÷ 55,000 units + $14.50 = $20.14 a unit) to benchmark performance quarter by quarter, attack the 13.5% returns problem — each returned unit destroys the $10.00 contribution — and renegotiate the $14.50 variable cost with suppliers amid 5.4% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 31,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 24,000 units against 55,000-unit output; discount modelling at $10.00 contribution; loan feasibility for the $450,000 ten-year bank loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $20.14 a unit to tackle the 13.5% returns rate and negotiate the $14.50 variable cost.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NGF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NGF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.43 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.63 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.57 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $260,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $430,000. Current assets 2025 = $210,000 + $175,000 + $55,000 = $440,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $430,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.43; 2025 = $440,000 ÷ $270,000 = 1.63. Stricter measure 2024 = ($430,000 − $260,000) ÷ $300,000 = $170,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.57; 2025 = ($440,000 − $210,000) ÷ $270,000 = $230,000 ÷ $270,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Short-term cover improved from 1.43 to 1.63, helped by current liabilities falling from $300,000 to $270,000 while current assets rose to $440,000. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.57 to 0.85, so NGF is far less reliant on selling stock to meet short-term debts — important while it services a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and funds the $720,000 fulfilment centre. However, trade receivables climbed from $140,000 to $175,000, tying up cash in customer balances; if these relate to corporate or wholesale orders paid late, NGF should tighten credit control. Inventories fell to $210,000, which suits a faster online model but leaves less cover if demand spikes.

Conclusion: NGF's financial position has improved. Both measures strengthened between 2024 and 2025 — 1.43 to 1.63 and 0.57 to 0.85 — and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so NGF should tighten credit control and protect cash flow while completing the $720,000 e-commerce fulfilment centre.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether NGF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NGF of operating its own e-commerce website alongside its three stores.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A dedicated e-commerce website lets NGF sell to the 58% of surveyed shoppers who would buy formalwear online, capture nationwide demand beyond Columbus and gather customer data such as body measurements and purchase history. This personalises recommendations, supports the online sizing guides 61% of shoppers want, and lifts sales without the rent, fittings and staffing cost of a fourth store while the $720,000 fulfilment centre comes online and the 6.8% growth in online apparel spending is pursued.

Disadvantage: Running its own website means NGF carries fulfilment, delivery and returns costs that stores do not — a 13.5% returns rate and 3.5 days average delivery currently erode margin unless the sizing guides and computer stock control cut parcels coming back. Every return also doubles handling on a $24.50 item with a $10.00 contribution, so the website only pays off if NGF drives the returns rate well below the current 13.5%, and it must fund the extra freight and customer service before online revenue is established.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NGF's research data, returns rate, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $14.25 and the combined 8.0% carrier fuel surcharge and 5.4% clothing input cost rise will affect NGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (from 4.5% to 5.75%): NGF's $450,000 ten-year bank loan, if variable-rate, will cost roughly 1.25% more a year, adding about $5,600 of annual interest and marginally raising the cost of any future equipment borrowing. Higher rates may also dampen discretionary spending on suits. The direct effect is real but modest, and NGF could fix the loan rate or renegotiate terms to cap the exposure.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.25 per hour): The national minimum wage rises from $13.42 to $14.25 per hour. That is a certain, recurring cost across NGF's wage bill — it hits every shift, every store and the fulfilment centre simultaneously, and democratic leadership, training and the productivity gains from automated fulfilment must offset it. NGF may need to review staffing levels or selective prices, and the wage rise may squeeze cash flow even as it builds the $720,000 automation investment.

Carrier fuel surcharge (+8.0%) and clothing input costs (+5.4%): A 5.4% rise on the $14.50 variable cost is about $0.78 per unit ($14.50 × 5.4% = $0.78), so the variable cost per unit rises and the $10.00 contribution absorbs some of it; the 8.0% fuel surcharge adds to delivery charges as well. Both are partly recoverable through sizing guides, carrier renegotiation and modest price increases.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is a certain, recurring, unavoidable cost on the whole workforce, while the input and carrier increases are partly controllable through supplier negotiation and lower returns, and the interest-rate increase can be fixed. NGF must prioritise productivity gains, scheduling efficiency and selective price rises alongside its $720,000 automation investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to NGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NGF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NGF with a well-justified judgment that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
